claims.text: Housing: the campaign's plan aims to add 40,000 owner-occupied homes Coloradans can afford, cutting the existing shortfall of such homes in half, with faster permitting, lower fees on homes under $600,000, down payment help, renter protections, and oversight of out-of-state investors and corporate landlords.
claims.sourceTitle: Campaign site: Affordable Homes and Communities

claims.text: Health care: the campaign's 'Healthy Colorado Plan' emphasizes prevention and primary care, more affordable insurance options, cheaper prescriptions, protections against surprise bills and medical debt, and a task force to shield care from federal cuts.
claims.sourceTitle: Campaign site: Healthcare

claims.text: Public safety: the campaign says he would support police hiring and training, sign and defend gun safety laws, send trained co-responders to addiction and mental health crises, tie bail decisions to public safety risk rather than finances, and create a Governor's Office of Safe Communities.
claims.sourceTitle: Campaign site: Public Safety

claims.text: The campaign's biography page says he is Colorado's Attorney General, clerked for U.S. Supreme Court Justice Ruth Bader Ginsburg, worked at the U.S. Department of Justice and the White House in the Clinton and Obama administrations, and chaired Governor Ritter's Innovation Council.
claims.sourceTitle: Campaign site: Meet Phil

claims.text: The campaign's home page lists these priorities: government accountability and transparency (ending waste and corruption); housing and cost of living; jobs, taxes and economic growth (cutting taxes); and law, order and public safety (backing law enforcement and putting victims first). Faith, freedom and nature appear as further headings with little detail on the page read.
claims.sourceTitle: Campaign site: home page

claims.text: The campaign's home page describes him as a husband, father and community servant who has overcome personal adversity, and says he has spent decades on front-line work supporting veterans, rescuing vulnerable people and building programs. It lists no prior elected office.
claims.sourceTitle: Campaign site: home page

claims.text: The campaign's biography page lists these priorities: lowering health care and prescription drug costs; reducing gun violence; protecting Colorado's public lands while addressing climate change; and working across party lines.
claims.sourceTitle: Campaign site: Meet John

claims.text: The campaign's biography page says he was elected Mayor of Denver and that he began as a geologist before opening Colorado's first brewpub and starting other small businesses. It says he ran for governor in 2010 and credits that work with results on job creation, climate and gun safety laws, and Medicaid expansion, but it does not state his terms or dates.
claims.sourceTitle: Campaign site: Meet John

claims.text: The campaign's issues page says he supports lower federal taxes, fewer regulations and more domestic energy production; more funding for law enforcement and an end to programs that release violent offenders early; and, on immigration, describes about 1.2 million people admitted legally each year after screening and says immigrants should be self-reliant and assimilate. For agriculture it favors fewer regulatory burdens and market-based solutions over expanded government programs.
claims.sourceTitle: Campaign site: Issues

claims.text: The campaign's home page describes a career as an aerospace engineer and leading a Colorado software company, and says he was elected to the Colorado House in 2018 and the Colorado Senate in 2022.
claims.sourceTitle: Campaign site: home page

claims.text: The Colorado General Assembly's member page lists him as a Republican state senator for District 4 with assignments to the Joint Technology, Local Government & Housing, and Transportation & Energy committees. The page read did not state service dates.
claims.sourceTitle: Colorado General Assembly: Senator Mark Baisley

claims.text: The campaign's About page emphasizes her record as Secretary of State on election security and access: it says she led efforts to criminalize threats against election workers and tampering with voting equipment, implemented automatic voter registration, and increased secure drop boxes. It says she will defend the rights and freedoms of all Coloradans and that she urged removing President Trump from the ballot.
claims.sourceTitle: Campaign site: About

claims.text: The campaign's About page says she was elected Colorado's 39th Secretary of State in 2018 and reelected in 2022, earlier directed the Colorado governor's Washington, D.C. office, practiced international anti-corruption law, and earned a law degree from the University of Pennsylvania.
claims.sourceTitle: Campaign site: About

claims.text: The campaign's home page lists these priorities: public safety and victims (holding repeat offenders accountable and working with local law enforcement); cost of living and taxpayers (reviewing state spending and cutting waste); investigating corruption and fraud; consumer protection, especially against scams targeting older adults; defending Colorado's water rights; and challenging federal overreach when Colorado's interests are harmed.
claims.sourceTitle: Campaign site: home page

claims.text: The campaign's home page says he served eight years in the U.S. Navy, has worked in prosecution for more than 20 years including as a consumer protection prosecutor in the Kansas Attorney General's Office, and was elected District Attorney of the Fourth Judicial District (El Paso and Teller counties) in 2020 and re-elected in 2024.
claims.sourceTitle: Campaign site: home page

claims.text: In the Denver Gazette's candidate questionnaire she says she defends Colorado's mail-ballot system as secure and accessible, would invest in physical and cybersecurity and work with county clerks without dismantling the system, would issue clearer campaign finance guidance and make donor and spending data easier to search, and would resist federal interference in state elections and challenge it in court when needed. On the 2024 ballot-access case she says the office should apply the law and court rulings without regard to candidate or party.
claims.sourceTitle: Denver Gazette candidate questionnaire: Secretary of State (Oct. 2, 2026)

claims.text: Her campaign site lists these priorities: protecting voting rights and expanding ballot access; election security and transparent, efficient administration; ensuring every eligible vote is counted; and limiting dark money.
claims.sourceTitle: Campaign site: home page and priorities

claims.text: In an interview with The Colorado Sun she said she supports automatically mailing ballots to active voters, says post-election audits and paper ballots are safeguards, does not take positions on ballot measures (including Amendment 84), and said Joe Biden won the 2020 election.
claims.sourceTitle: Colorado Sun voter guide: Secretary of State (Oct. 7, 2026)

claims.text: The Colorado Sun reports she has been Jefferson County clerk and recorder since 2023, led the nonprofit Colorado Common Cause from 2018 to 2021, and is an attorney. Her campaign site describes the same county role and the Common Cause role without dates.
claims.sourceTitle: Colorado Sun voter guide: Secretary of State (Oct. 7, 2026)

claims.text: In the Denver Gazette's candidate questionnaire he says he favors one-day in-person voting with government-issued ID and paper ballots; if mail voting continues he would add citizenship checks, stricter ID and signature standards and documented chain of custody, and reduce electronic voting systems. He would make filings searchable in plain language, close dark-money loopholes, and publish data on late filings and enforcement. He says elections are a state responsibility and he would resist federal overreach while allowing limited cooperation on shared threats. On the 2024 ballot-access case he says he would have defended ballot access and applied the law evenly.
claims.sourceTitle: Denver Gazette candidate questionnaire: Secretary of State (Oct. 2, 2026)

claims.text: His campaign site's issues page proposes a statewide voting holiday, in-person voting in every precinct, voter ID, paper ballots only, citizen-run hand counts that clerks could choose to use, cleaning voter rolls, moving public records to an auditable blockchain ledger, and reducing business regulation.
claims.sourceTitle: Campaign site: issues

claims.text: In an interview with The Colorado Sun he said he opposes automatic mailing of ballots and would return to absentee voting with a stated reason (which would need a change in state law), supports periodic voter-roll reviews, supports Amendment 84, and said he does not know who won the 2020 election. The Sun adds that no evidence of widespread fraud in the 2020 election has been revealed.
claims.sourceTitle: Colorado Sun voter guide: Secretary of State (Oct. 7, 2026)

claims.text: His campaign site says he was born in Colorado Springs, lived in Kazakhstan for about 15 years as a child, earned a management and marketing degree and an MBA at CSU-Pueblo, ran a financial-services practice and a consulting firm, and turned to full-time election-integrity work after 2020. The Colorado Sun reports he was a Libertarian until last year. The sources list no prior elected office.
claims.sourceTitle: Campaign site: home and biography

claims.text: In the Denver Gazette's candidate questionnaire he says he would roll back mail voting, with exceptions for voters with disabilities, and make in-person voting the main method; would apply clear public campaign finance standards equally and allow fixes for good-faith mistakes; and would cooperate with federal agencies on cybersecurity but keep Colorado in control. On the 2024 ballot-access case he says he would have kept the candidate on the ballot unless a clear legal ruling required removal.
claims.sourceTitle: Denver Gazette candidate questionnaire: Secretary of State (Oct. 2, 2026)

claims.text: The questionnaire describes him as a small business owner and political volunteer.
claims.sourceTitle: Denver Gazette candidate questionnaire: Secretary of State (Oct. 2, 2026)

claims.text: In the Denver Gazette's candidate questionnaire she says she supports mail ballots and vote centers, with electronic return only for voters with specific needs such as military and overseas voters; cites paper ballots and risk-limiting audits as safeguards; would create a working group with public-interest groups to improve campaign finance enforcement and make TRACER better for analysis; is wary of coordinating with federal agencies; and on the 2024 ballot-access case says she would have let the lawsuit proceed and asked for a quick decision.
claims.sourceTitle: Denver Gazette candidate questionnaire: Secretary of State (Oct. 2, 2026)

claims.text: The questionnaire describes her as a longtime advocate for better voting methods and a volunteer lobbyist with the League of Women Voters, and notes a 2024 Colorado Sun guest opinion in which she proposed an alternative to vacancy committee elections.
claims.sourceTitle: Denver Gazette candidate questionnaire: Secretary of State (Oct. 2, 2026)

claims.text: In the Denver Gazette's candidate questionnaire he says he would invest more state money inside Colorado in affordable housing, infrastructure, renewable energy and small businesses, protect PERA, make government more transparent and return unclaimed property proactively, and oppose repeatedly spending that money to close budget gaps. He says PERA is about 69% funded and on track to eliminate its unfunded liability by 2048, and points to his record of increasing state contributions.
claims.sourceTitle: Denver Gazette candidate questionnaire: State Treasurer (Oct. 2, 2026)

claims.text: His campaign site lists priorities of affordable housing for workers such as nurses, teachers and firefighters, investing in infrastructure and clean energy to lower utility bills, directing state investment to Colorado businesses, and moving state Treasury funds into Colorado (it cites Vermont, Illinois and Nevada as examples).
claims.sourceTitle: Campaign site: home page

claims.text: His campaign site says he has about ten years in the state legislature, including four years on the Joint Budget Committee and service as its chair, and that he earlier worked for U.S. Senator Ken Salazar. The Gazette describes him as a state senator and chair of the Joint Budget Committee.
claims.sourceTitle: Campaign site: home page and expertise

claims.text: The Colorado General Assembly's member page lists him as a Democratic senator for District 26 and Vice Chair of the Senate Appropriations Committee and of the Joint Budget Committee. The campaign site and the Gazette call him chair of the Joint Budget Committee, so the official page may be out of date; it gives no service dates.
claims.sourceTitle: Colorado General Assembly: Senator Jeff Bridges

claims.text: In the Denver Gazette's candidate questionnaire he says he would maximize taxpayer dollars and advocate for families under affordability pressure, and that the state should do more with less. He opposes the state using unclaimed property money for general spending, which he calls a tax increase without a public vote. On PERA he says the state must meet its obligations to workers, manage risk and pursue strong returns, and he calls for lower investment-management costs and fewer large salaries and bonuses.
claims.sourceTitle: Denver Gazette candidate questionnaire: State Treasurer (Oct. 2, 2026)

claims.text: His campaign site's home page gives one broad theme, making Colorado more affordable, and links a launch video; the home page lists no detailed policy positions.
claims.sourceTitle: Campaign site: home page

claims.text: In the questionnaire he describes himself as a former Colorado Senate president and current Fremont County commissioner. The Colorado General Assembly page that could document his legislative service returned outdated information (a 2017-2018 listing), so it is not cited.
claims.sourceTitle: Denver Gazette candidate questionnaire: State Treasurer (Oct. 2, 2026)

claims.text: In the Denver Gazette's candidate questionnaire he says he would act as a fiduciary for taxpayers rather than an advocate for higher spending, protect dedicated funds, increase transparency in the state's roughly $17 billion of investments, defend TABOR and reduce reliance on debt, speed up returns of unclaimed property, and end or sharply limit transfers from the unclaimed property fund. On PERA he says it is about 69% funded with roughly $30 billion unfunded and supports closing the defined-benefit plan to new hires in favor of defined-contribution accounts, more transparent actuarial assumptions and no new benefit increases.
claims.sourceTitle: Denver Gazette candidate questionnaire: State Treasurer (Oct. 2, 2026)

claims.text: The questionnaire says years of running a small business shaped his view that every tax dollar has a real cost, and that he has studied state and municipal finance closely.
claims.sourceTitle: Denver Gazette candidate questionnaire: State Treasurer (Oct. 2, 2026)
